channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] A China-linked crew broke into self-hosted Git servers — and walked out of a Taiwanese automation vendor with the source code to its SCADA and HMI tooling
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Acronis Threat Research Unit research published on 13 September, and reported by outlets on 14 and 15 September, describes a campaign attributed with moderate confidence to a China-linked actor they call Red Heron. Acronis observed the group exploiting CVE-2026-60004, the critical (CVSS 9.8) remote-code-execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea that Gitea fixed in 1.27.1 on 27 July, between 29 July and 4 August 2026, when it found the actor’s staging server. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 25 August with a 28 August federal deadline, now passed. Researchers observed scanning of 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and confirmed 11 compromised targets in five countries — Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka — in a target set spanning industrial automation, renewable energy, aerospace, telecommunications, defence and government. The manufacturing victim is the one that matters here: a Taiwanese industrial-automation company from which the actor pulled hundreds of repositories, including a SCADA/HMI tool used in industrial control environments, IoT platform integrations, a network sniffer, server configurations and internal business applications. At a Canadian renewable-energy operator Acronis counted 22 separate exploitation sessions, mapping of internal systems, three SSH key entries planted for persistence and 61 database dumps. On compromised hosts the actor deployed a custom C++ Linux implant the researchers name JITTERLY, with more than thirty post-exploitation commands, and an embedded LD_PRELOAD rootkit, SIXZUT, that hides files, processes and network connections. Nothing published indicates a control system was manipulated or a production line stopped, and that is not the risk being described. This is theft of the engineering substrate — the authoritative source for automation software that a vendor’s customers then install on their plant floors. The operator’s exposure is second-order and arrives later: an adversary reading the source of the HMI and SCADA products running in your plant knows their authentication logic, their protocol handling and their update mechanism before you do. The victims are not named, and there is no public indication that remediation is complete. The one development since is indirect: on 21 September GreyNoise assessed, on the basis of shared command-and-control infrastructure, malware and tactics including the same Gitea flaw, that the actor it observed exploiting Zyxel GS1900 switches (see the advisory below) is the same as, or related to, Red Heron. That is an inference by a second vendor, not a confirmation, and Acronis has not updated its own report. - Acronis Threat Research Unit report of 13 Sep 2026 (primary, re-read 22 Sep 2026), reported by The Hacker News on 14 Sep 2026 and by Industrial Cyber on 15 Sep 2026 — the CVE’s KEV listing per the CISA catalogue; the overlap with the Zyxel GS1900 actor is GreyNoise’s assessment of 21 Sep 2026 - Acronis report 13 Sep 2026; outlet reporting 14–15 Sep 2026; exploitation dated from 29 Jul 2026

item.title: [Medium] New Settra ransomware hit a manufacturer this month — and wiped the recovery partitions before it encrypted anything
item.category: Incident — Ransomware at an unnamed manufacturer, IT-side, confirmed by incident responders
item.description: Huntress published incident-response findings on 17 September on a new ransomware variant it calls Settra, drawn from two cases it investigated: a consumer-services and retail organisation in July and a manufacturing company in September 2026. Neither victim, nor its country, is named. In both cases the operators kept access through the MeshAgent remote-management agent (renamed to blend in during the July case) and named the encryptor after the victim’s own domain. The September intrusion went further: the attackers loaded the vulnerable gdrv.sys driver to impair security tooling, then worked through the recovery options one by one — disabling Windows Recovery with reagentc, deleting recovery partitions with a diskpart script, clearing event logs and overwriting free space with cipher — before encrypting files with a .locked_wip extension. Huntress says it did not confirm the initial access vector in either case, so reports pointing to VPN compromise and credential misuse remain unconfirmed for these incidents, and it describes the actors as capable rather than sophisticated. No operational-technology or production impact is reported. The relevance for a plant is the sequence rather than the brand: remote-management tooling nobody approved, a signed-but-vulnerable driver, then the deliberate removal of local recovery, which is exactly the path that turns a Windows HMI, historian or engineering workstation from a reimage into a rebuild. - Huntress research “New Settra ransomware variant” — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive and Infosecurity Magazine. Victims are unnamed; findings are Huntress’s own incident-response observations - Huntress published 17 Sep 2026; trade coverage 18 Sep 2026; incidents July and September 2026

item.title: [Medium] Panzer claims an Italian kitchen manufacturer — the detail worth your attention is the ESXi build, not the claim
item.category: Incident — Ransomware claim against a manufacturer, unconfirmed by the victim
item.description: Fresh analysis published on 10 September fills out the Panzer ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in August 2026 and has claimed victims in 11 countries in its first month. Two of the listed victims are Italian: kitchen manufacturer Doimo Cucine, posted on 17 August with roughly 30 GB of data claimed exfiltrated, and NTE Italia, a telecom engineering firm rather than a manufacturer, posted on 21 August with roughly 16 GB claimed. Neither company has confirmed an incident, researchers explicitly describe the listings as attacker claims rather than forensic proof, and no production halt has been confirmed at either. Treat the victim claims accordingly. What is worth acting on is the capability description: alongside Windows and Linux, Panzer ships builds for VMware ESXi and FreeBSD, and double extortion is standard. Hypervisor-level encryption is the part that lengthens industrial recovery, because in most plants the MES, historian, SCADA servers, batch and recipe management and the engineering-workstation images are virtual machines on a small number of ESXi hosts. Encrypt the hosts and every one of those goes at once, regardless of how well segmented the guests were from each other. - Industrial Cyber analysis of the Panzer RaaS operation, drawing on researcher tracking of its leak site — victim claims are attacker-sourced and are reported here as unverified - Victims listed 17 and 21 Aug 2026; analysis published 10 Sep 2026; no victim confirmation as of this edition

item.title: [Medium] Resolved, but not costless — Boston Scientific has manufacturing and shipping back, and has confirmed the August attack will land a “material” hit on its Q3 and full-year guidance
item.category: Incident — Resolved: IT compromise that had halted manufacturing and shipping
item.description: In its 9 September update Boston Scientific reported substantial recovery from the cybersecurity incident it identified on 25 August — manufacturing and sterilisation largely functional, shipping running above normal levels to clear the backlog — and stated in the same update that manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping operations are now fully restored, with some customers possibly still seeing temporary delays. In the same update the company confirmed the incident will have a “material” effect on its third-quarter and full-year sales and earnings-per-share guidance, with the quantified figure due at the 28 October earnings call. Independent assessment by CrowdStrike and other third-party experts found no evidence of ongoing threat activity and no evidence that product development, manufacturing systems or cloud platforms were compromised; unauthorised access is assessed as having been limited to internal-facing IT infrastructure. Remote cardiac-device monitoring, which had also been disrupted, is likewise restored. The company has still not named an actor, confirmed ransomware, or disclosed root cause. Note what has and has not closed: the operational disruption has ended, the financial consequence has not been sized, and that ordering is the normal shape of these events rather than an anomaly. This page previously carried the incident as an ongoing disruption with no recovery date; that framing is now superseded. The operational lesson survives the resolution intact, and it is the reason to keep the card on the board rather than the reason to panic: production stopped for roughly two weeks without anything published suggesting a controller, DCS or plant network was touched, because the systems that tell a factory what to build and where to ship it live on the IT side of the boundary. - Boston Scientific corporate statement “Update on recent cybersecurity incident” of 9 Sep 2026, with the independent assessment attributed by the company to CrowdStrike — corroborated by the company’s SEC Form 8-K, HIPAA Journal, MedTech Dive, Industrial Cyber, SecurityWeek and Cybersecurity Dive - Incident identified 25 Aug 2026; SEC Form 8-K 26 Aug 2026; shipping restart 3 Sep 2026; full restoration of manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping confirmed by the company update of 9 Sep 2026, which also confirmed the material guidance impact; financial detail due 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] What a refusal to pay actually publishes: risk assessments, site documentation and plaintext credentials
item.category: Incident — Refusal to pay, then publication of infrastructure documentation
item.description: Rhysida released the data it took from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set is around 5.79 TB across roughly 1.44 million files, and beyond personnel and payroll records it is reported to include critical-infrastructure vulnerability analyses and plaintext credentials for administrator accounts and connected systems. Berlin’s own timeline is the operationally useful part: outflow first detected 7 August, continuing to around 12 August, with affected departments not physically disconnected until 14 August. For a manufacturer the read-across is direct. Your network diagrams, cell layouts, PLC program archives and OEM VPN credentials are rarely held in only one place — copies sit with machine builders, systems integrators, insurers and customers running supplier assurance, and a breach at any of them publishes your plant without touching your plant. - Berlin state administration statements — reported by Help Net Security and Security Affairs - Breach and refusal to pay reported 1 Sep 2026; data published by the actor 4 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A North Korea-linked implant lived inside the HAProxy load balancer at a South Korean automotive firm — where TLS ends and EDR never looks
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Nation-state espionage at an automotive company, IT-side, no OT impact
item.description: Rapid7 Labs research, reported by Dark Reading on 16 September, describes a previously undocumented Linux espionage toolkit that Rapid7 attributes with medium confidence to a North Korean state actor, possibly APT37, and that was found at two South Korean organisations, one in media and one in automotive manufacturing. The core component, which Rapid7 calls TED, is a malicious plugin built into HAProxy, the open-source load balancer that terminates TLS in front of web applications. From that position it can read decrypted traffic, steal session cookies and credentials, inject scripts into pages and run commands, all while the load balancer keeps doing its job. A companion implant, curlRAT, is a trojanised copy of ordinary system daemons such as crond and sshd that talks to its operators over libcurl. Rapid7 says the tooling generates no unusual processes, no unexpected outbound connections and no log entries of its own, and that it scrubs logs and connection counters selectively. Initial access is not confirmed; Rapid7 judges it was most likely through exposed groupware or mail portals. Nothing published indicates that production systems or control networks were touched, and the stated objective on the automotive side is manufacturing-technology intelligence rather than disruption. The relevance for a plant is architectural: the reverse proxies and load balancers in front of MES portals, vendor-access gateways and historian web front-ends occupy exactly this position, they are typically Linux appliances outside endpoint-detection coverage, and they are trusted precisely because they are boring. - Rapid7 Labs technical report on the TED backdoor and curlRAT — reported by Dark Reading; attribution and victim count are Rapid7’s - Reported 16 Sep 2026; Rapid7 says the activity dates back to early 2025

item.title: [Medium] 1,183 manufacturers listed in seven months, up 40 percent — and half of it from crews that did not exist two years ago
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics, leak-site derived
item.description: Black Kite’s 2026 Manufacturing & Distribution Ransomware Report, covered on 17 and 18 September, counts 1,183 new ransomware incidents against manufacturers in the first seven months of 2026, a 40 percent rise on the same period in 2025, against 5,237 disclosed victims across manufacturing and distribution since January 2023. Two findings are worth more than the headline number. The first is churn: about half of this year’s attacks came from groups that did not exist two years ago, with The Gentlemen — unheard of until recently — claiming 142 manufacturing victims by mid-year, roughly 12 percent of the annual total, behind Qilin and ahead of Akira, DragonForce and INC Ransom. Defending against a named group’s tradecraft is a losing strategy when the names turn over this fast. The second is geography: the United States accounts for 412 attacks but has fallen from 52 percent of the total to 35 percent, while Europe rose 85 percent year on year to 369 — Germany 77, Italy 57, the UK 43, France 40 — and the rest of the world nearly doubled to 402. European and Asian plants that treated this as an American problem no longer can. Distribution alone logged 95 incidents in the first half of 2026 against 196 for all of 2025. Read the counts for what they are: leak-site and disclosure data, which measures claimed victims rather than confirmed operational impact, and the report’s illustrative cases — Jaguar Land Rover’s plant shutdown and the Cleo campaign — are 2025 events used as context, not new ones. - Black Kite “2026 Manufacturing & Distribution Ransomware Report” — figures as reported by SecurityWeek, Industrial Cyber and Cybersecurity Dive; the report itself was not read directly - Reported 17–18 Sep 2026; data covers January 2023 to July 2026

item.title: [Info] Only 13% of network segments that hold OT devices are OT-only — Forescout’s count across 47,700 segments
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Exposure research, segmentation telemetry
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published an analysis on 22 September of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices at 209 organisations. Of the segments that contain OT devices, only 13 percent held OT alone; the rest shared the segment with IT or IoT equipment. The average segment held 54 devices performing four different functions, and the most common mixing Forescout saw was IP cameras sharing segments with workstations, printers and servers. The largest average “blast radius” — how much an attacker can reach from one compromised device — was in business and professional services, healthcare, and oil and gas; Forescout does not single out manufacturing in that ranking, so read the headline as a cross-industry figure. This is exposure research drawn from the vendor’s own device telemetry, not an incident. It is on this page because it describes the plant-floor norm most assessments find: the camera, the badge reader, the UPS card and the line PC sitting in the same VLAN as the controllers, so a foothold on the least-managed device is a foothold next to the process. - Forescout Vedere Labs research (primary, read 24 Sep 2026) — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Two vendor surveys, one gap: nearly nine in ten manufacturers think they could contain an incident, and only one in five respondents has a complete OT asset inventory
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor surveys, self-reported
item.description: Two industrial-vendor surveys were published on 22 and 23 September, and both are self-reported, so treat them as a picture of what respondents believe rather than as measured incident data. Rockwell Automation’s survey of more than 1,500 manufacturers across 17 industrial nations, with annual revenues between $100 million and $30 billion, found that nearly nine in ten believe their company could contain a cyber incident, while nearly half reported a breach or attack in the past 12 months and more than a third named cyber risk as the top obstacle to growth. Honeywell’s 2026 OT cybersecurity benchmark, released on 22 September and drawn from more than 600 industrial security leaders across sectors, found 88 percent described their OT programmes as mature, while only 21 percent reported a complete inventory of their OT assets and just 33 percent had fully integrated OT into a centralised security operations centre. Respondents’ most significant incidents averaged 16.2 hours of downtime. Honeywell’s release does not break manufacturing out as its own sector. The useful reading for a plant is the distance between the two sets of answers: confidence in containment is high, and the basic inventory that containment depends on is mostly incomplete. - Honeywell press release of 22 Sep 2026 (primary, read 24 Sep 2026); Rockwell Automation survey as reported by Cybersecurity Dive (23 Sep 2026) - Honeywell 22 Sep 2026; Rockwell reporting 23 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Manufacturing has been the most-hit sector in ransomware reporting for years, and the August record extends the trend. The operational reality behind the number is the one this sector keeps relearning: IT restoration takes hours, production restart takes days. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For a plant this reframes the whole conversation. Rather than asking how to keep an attacker off the cell network, it asks where a compromise could produce a physical consequence and whether the design already forecloses it — hardwired E-stops, mechanical limits, independent safety instrumented systems. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A credential-harvesting campaign built and executed by autonomous agents in under six hours
item.category: Threat intel — Autonomous agent frameworks in live intrusion operations
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group used an autonomous multi-agent framework to stand up and run a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours, with agents handling stages that used to take an operator days. GTIG separately observed actors targeting proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and co-opting victim cloud tenants to run their own workloads. Its guidance is to assume every threat actor is now using AI somewhere. For manufacturers the exposure is the credential layer around production: integrator and OEM support accounts, engineering-workstation logins, MES and ERP access, and the federated identity that increasingly sits behind vendor remote sessions into the cell. - Google Threat Intelligence Group research reported by The Hacker News, including comment from GTIG’s John Hultquist - Published and reported 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A second Check Point Management Server flaw was a zero-day for two months — CVE-2026-93616 is exploited, in KEV, and fixed only on 22 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management plane, exploited zero-day, CISA KEV
item.description: Check Point disclosed on 22 September that CVE-2026-93616, a pre-authentication path-traversal flaw in the Security Management web service rated CVSS 9.8, had been used in what it describes as a handful of pinpointed attacks on 23 July 2026 — roughly two months before a fix became available on 22 September. Reporting on the advisory describes the flaw as letting an unauthenticated attacker upload and execute scripts, and lists Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent as affected. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. This is not CVE-2026-91843, the over-long-username login flaw on the card below, which remains unexploited; the two sit on the same server and need to be tracked separately. No victims, sectors or attribution have been published, and no manufacturing target is named. The weight for a plant is the same as with 91843, now with confirmed use: the management server writes and pushes the policy for every gateway it manages, including the enterprise-to-plant boundary, so an attacker who held it since July could have changed that boundary without touching a gateway directly. - Check Point security advisory of 22 Sep 2026 (vendor blog) and the CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026; affected-product and hotfix detail as reported by Help Net Security and SecurityAffairs (23 Sep 2026) - Exploitation observed 23 Jul 2026; fix and KEV listing 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two more exploited edge platforms in KEV: Arista’s VeloCloud SD-WAN orchestrator at CVSS 10, and F5 BIG-IP APM acting as an OAuth server
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited edge platforms, CISA KEV
item.description: CISA’s 22 September KEV update added four actively exploited flaws, all with a 25 September federal deadline: the two Check Point vulnerabilities on this page and two more on edge platforms. Arista Security Advisory 0183 of 22 September covers CVE-2026-93952, an improper-input-validation flaw in the on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator rated CVSS v3.1 10.0 that Arista says is known to be actively exploited. It is reachable only where certificate-based Edge-to-Orchestrator authentication is configured, and needs no tenant or operator credentials. Fixed builds are 5.2.3.16 and later and 6.4.2.8 and later; Arista lists no fix yet for the 6.1.x and 7.0.x trains, and its hosted orchestrator is already patched. Arista has published indicators including the files .vcnode.js and vc-sysmond and the HTTP header x-vc-opt. F5’s CVE-2026-94127 (K000162605) is a CVSS 9.8 heap overflow in BIG-IP APM that gives unauthenticated code execution, but only where a virtual server combines an APM access policy with an OAuth profile so that APM acts as an OAuth authorisation server; F5 has issued engineering hotfixes and Rapid7 reports no confirmed public proof-of-concept. Neither has a named manufacturing victim. They belong on a plant page because of position: an SD-WAN orchestrator pushes configuration to every site edge it manages, plants included, and an APM gateway is often how remote staff and suppliers get in. - Arista Security Advisory 0183 and F5 K000162605 (vendor primaries); CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026; Rapid7 analysis of CVE-2026-94127; reporting by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Advisories and KEV listing 22 Sep 2026; reporting 22–23 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The VPN client on the machine builder’s laptop: a CVSS 9.6 flaw in the Lenze/IXON client runs commands as root or SYSTEM
item.category: Critical Advisory — Machine-builder remote-access client, no known exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-089 on 21 September for CVE-2026-75925 in the Lenze VPN Client, the IXON-based client used with Lenze’s x500 IoT Gateway for remote access to machines. Versions 1.0.0 through 1.4.6 fail to neutralise line-ending (CRLF) sequences in configuration values that are written to files read by privileged processes, so an attacker can inject extra directives and run commands as root or SYSTEM. The configuration interface does not check authentication, and injected settings survive a restart. The flaw is rated CVSS 3.1 9.6 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C) — reachable over the network with no privileges, but requiring a user action. The fix is version 1.4.7, and the vendor’s cloud now blocks older clients with an error message, which forces the update for anyone who connects. The advisory does not report exploitation. The reason this matters more than its product name suggests is where the client runs: on the service laptops of OEM and machine-builder engineers who connect to many customers’ machines. A client compromised with SYSTEM rights on that laptop sits at the start of the tunnel into your cell. - CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-089 (primary, read 24 Sep 2026) - Published 21 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 9.8 flaw in lwIP’s MQTT client — the open-source network stack inside a long tail of controllers, IO modules and gateways
item.category: Critical Advisory — Embedded TCP/IP stack, downstream exposure unknown
item.description: CISA published two advisories on 22 September for lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack embedded in a large share of industrial devices. The first, ICSA-26-265-01, covers CVE-2026-87121, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client application rated CVSS 9.8, reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay; the second covers a double-free flaw reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security. No exploitation has been reported. What neither advisory can tell you is which products are affected, because lwIP is a component: only devices whose firmware ships the MQTT client application are exposed to the first flaw, and each device vendor has to establish that and publish its own notice. For a plant that makes this a supply-chain tracking job rather than a patch. The likely carriers are the MQTT-speaking IIoT gateways, smart sensors, edge controllers and remote IO added for data collection — frequently the least inventoried devices on the floor. - CISA ICS advisories of 22 Sep 2026, as listed by Chemical Facility Security News; CVE identifier and score per public CVE records - Published 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 22 September batch: Siemens SIPLUS and SIMATIC inherit a Linux kernel flaw, SIMOVE and Industrial Edge are re-posted, and OpenPLC gets an XSS advisory
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS batch, Siemens republications and OpenPLC
item.description: Alongside the two lwIP advisories, CISA’s 22 September ICS release republished a set of Siemens advisories and added one for OpenPLC. For manufacturers the relevant Siemens items are: SIPLUS and SIMATIC products affected by “Copy Fail”, a third-party Linux vulnerability inherited through the embedded operating system rather than a defect in Siemens’ own code; SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT, the path-traversal flaw (CVE-2026-67367) that Siemens first published on 8 September and that has its own card below; Industrial Edge Management, from the same September Siemens cycle; and WTV676 and WTV776 devices, with an improper-input-validation flaw. The OpenPLC advisory covers a cross-site-scripting flaw in the Autonomy Logic OpenPLC runtime, reported by researchers at Secnora — minor in severity, but OpenPLC turns up in labs, training rigs and small retrofit cells. None of the batch is reported as exploited and none is in KEV. The practical value of a CISA republication is that it pushes the Siemens items into the feeds and scanners that read CISA rather than Siemens ProductCERT. - CISA ICS advisories of 22 Sep 2026, as listed by Chemical Facility Security News; underlying Siemens ProductCERT advisories - CISA publication 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw enters KEV after 996 units in 48 countries had their configurations and credential hashes pulled — the exploit needs LAN access, which a plant cell provides
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, cell-level managed switches
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 21 September with a 24 September federal deadline. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series smart managed switches — GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2 — that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the local network run operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel fixed it in June in firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and the per-model equivalents. The same day GreyNoise published what it describes as the first documented in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, assessed as a Chinese speaker, compromised 996 switches across 48 countries, led by Italy (133), the United States (129), Taiwan (123) and France, using a PyArmor-obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level password hashes over TFTP; 564 of the affected switches still used factory-default credentials. GreyNoise also assesses, from shared infrastructure and malware, that the actor is the same as or related to Red Heron, the group in this edition’s top story; that is an inference, not a confirmation. The manufacturing angle is that GS1900s are exactly the small, inexpensive managed switches found in machine cabinets, cells and OEM-supplied skids, and a flaw that needs LAN access is not a barrier to an attacker who is already on a plant or contractor network. A stolen switch configuration hands over VLAN layout, management addresses and credential hashes that are frequently reused across the site. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, GreyNoise research of 21 Sep 2026 and the Zyxel security advisory for GS1900-series switches of 16 Jun 2026 - Zyxel fix 16 Jun 2026; KEV addition and GreyNoise report 21 Sep 2026; federal deadline 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two exploited Cisco zero-days in three days — and the worse one sits on the box that decides what gets onto your plant network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, identity and mail edge
item.description: Cisco published an advisory on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC rated CVSS 10.0, in which an unauthenticated attacker reaches the web-based management interface through an API endpoint with insufficient authentication. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. Cisco’s PSIRT states it is aware of active exploitation. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 September with a 19 September federal deadline — three days, which is unusually short, and now passed. There are no workarounds; restricting management traffic with infrastructure access lists is the interim control, and Cisco notes that ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and must be migrated rather than patched. Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency issued its own alert on 21 September. Two days earlier, on 14 September, Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76461, a SQL-injection flaw in Secure Email Gateway’s AsyncOS email parsing rated CVSS 9.8, where a crafted message alone yields arbitrary SQL and command execution as root with no user interaction; it went into KEV the same day with a 17 September deadline, and Shadowserver counted more than 400 exposed appliances. Neither carries an actor attribution, and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed for either. The manufacturing relevance is the first one’s position rather than its score: ISE is commonly the 802.1X and network-access-control policy engine that decides which devices and which remote sessions are allowed onto plant and industrial-DMZ segments, so control of it is control of the admission decision. - Cisco security advisories cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 (16 Sep 2026) and cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX (14 Sep 2026), with the CISA KEV catalogue — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Cybersecurity Dive - Secure Email Gateway advisory and KEV 14 Sep 2026; ISE advisory and KEV 16 Sep 2026; version detail reported 17 Sep 2026; both KEV deadlines passed by 19 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] One crafted network message can stop an ABB Freelance controller — no credentials needed, and the fix is already sitting in update rollups many sites never installed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor advisory, process DCS, no known exploitation
item.description: ABB published advisory 7PAA010706 on 18 September for CVE-2023-5778, a flaw in how Freelance DCS controllers handle an inconsistent length parameter: a specially crafted message sent over the network, without authentication, makes the controller stop. The CVE was reserved in 2023 and published only now. Affected are the Freelance DCP, AC 700F, AC 800F and AC 900F controllers on Freelance 2013 and earlier, 2013 SP1, 2016, 2016 SP1, 2019 and 2019 SP1; the vendor’s machine-readable advisory scores it CVSS 7.5 under v3.1. Fixes already exist in shipped update rollups — 2013 SP1 RU06, 2016 SP1 RU07, 2019 SP1 RU03 or later, and 2019 SP1 FP1 — and Freelance 2024 is not affected. ABB says it had no reports of exploitation when it issued the advisory. Freelance is a common choice for process lines in chemical, pharmaceutical and batch manufacturing, and many of those installations run long-lived releases that never received later rollups. The risk is a controller stop on a running process, available to anyone who can reach the control network. - ABB cybersecurity advisory 7PAA010706 (CSAF) and ABB alerts and notifications index - Advisory and CVE published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Moxa TN-4500B switches: an over-long username at the web login crashes authentication and takes the switch out of service, no credentials required
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor advisory, industrial Ethernet switch, no known exploitation
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579, an out-of-bounds write in the TN-4500B series of industrial Ethernet switches running firmware 2.0 and earlier. The flaw is in how the web login handles the username field: a remote, unauthenticated attacker who sends a specially crafted over-long value triggers a buffer overflow, crashing the authentication process and causing a denial of service. Moxa scores it CVSS 8.8 under v4.0, with high availability impact and a lesser integrity impact, and fixes it in firmware 2.1. The vulnerability was reported by a researcher named Mask Lu; no exploitation is reported. The TN-4500B is an EN 50155-rated managed switch built for rolling stock and harsh environments, and it also turns up in automated guided vehicles, mobile equipment and outdoor plant where vibration and temperature rule out ordinary switches. A switch that can be knocked over from the network by anyone who can reach its login page is a single point of failure for whatever it connects. - Moxa product security advisory MPSA-252620 - Released 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Rockwell extends its lock-out recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850 — the notice exists because attackers have been setting passwords on exposed PLCs that never had one
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, small-site PLCs, exploitation is the premise
item.description: Rockwell Automation revised security notice SD1790 to revision 5.0 on 18 September, extending its hardening guidance and its instructions for restoring access to a controller when the password is unknown from the MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers. There is no CVE. The notice, first issued on 30 July, references the FBI public service announcement of the same date describing attackers remotely altering the configuration of internet-exposed PLCs, changing their IP addresses and setting passwords where none existed, so that operators lose access to their own controllers. Revision 5.0 adds no new incident data; it widens the set of products with a documented recovery path. The recommendations are the standard ones, which is not a reason to skip them: remove controllers from internet exposure, put remote access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords before someone else does, keep offline backups of the program, disable the controller’s HTTP server and keep firmware current. The Micro800 family is the low-cost PLC in packaging machines, conveyors, small process skids and OEM equipment across manufacturing, and it is disproportionately likely to have been commissioned by a machine builder, connected through a cellular router for support, and never looked at again. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790, revision 5.0, referencing the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026 - Original notice 30 Jul 2026; revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Three exploited Linux kernel flaws enter KEV with a three-day deadline — the plant exposure is the Linux inside gateways and panel PCs
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, CISA KEV, embedded Linux
item.description: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 September, with a federal remediation date of 21 September, now passed: CVE-2025-39682 in the kernel TLS receive path, CVE-2026-53266, an out-of-bounds write in the ebtables SNAT target, and CVE-2025-39964, a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface. Published severity scores for the three differ widely between sources, so none is carried here. These are local flaws that help an attacker who already has a foothold, not remote entry points. No actor, target or sector has been named, and there is no public detail on how they are being exploited. The manufacturing relevance is where Linux runs unnoticed: industrial edge gateways, HMIs and panel PCs, historians and Linux-based OT appliances, whose vendor firmware typically trails upstream kernel fixes by months. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and CISA alerts of 18 Sep 2026 — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 18 Sep 2026; reporting 19 Sep 2026; federal deadline 21 Sep 2026 (passed); status re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 17 September batch: a Mitsubishi GX Works3 authentication flaw at CVSS 8.8 that reaches the control program itself
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA’s bulletin for Thursday 17 September listed eight items: seven new ICS advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update, covering Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3, Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The one to read first here is ICSA-26-260-02: CVE-2026-15688, an authentication algorithm vulnerability in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, rated CVSS 8.8 under v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, affecting all versions, and listed by CISA under Critical Manufacturing. A summary of the advisory describes it as a local authentication bypass permitting tampering with the control program — which is to say, on the engineering software that writes logic to your MELSEC controllers. Bransys ELD, the only other advisory whose detail is confirmed, covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential flaws in an electronic logging device for commercial trucking, CVE-2026-86520 at 7.5 alongside CVE-2026-86689 and CVE-2026-77960, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. Scores for the rest of the batch are now in CISA’s public CSAF files, and all list Critical Manufacturing among affected sectors. ICSA-26-260-04 republishes a 2025 Schneider advisory: CVE-2025-6625, a crafted FTP command that causes a denial of service on Modicon M340 and several X80 Ethernet modules (CVSS 7.5 v3.1, 8.7 v4; M340 firmware fixed in SV3.70). ICSA-26-260-05 covers NetBotz 5 command injection CVE-2026-13336 (6.4 v3.1, 7.3 v4) and SQL injection CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0; the NetBotz and PowerChute advisories republish Schneider notices originally dated 11 August, and the Edgenius advisory one from 25 June. ICSA-26-260-06 is the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel privilege escalation, CVE-2026-31431 (7.8), in ABB Ability Edgenius, fixed in 3.2.4.1. ICSA-26-260-07 is PowerChute Serial Shutdown CVE-2026-13348, an excessive-authentication-attempts flaw (5.3 v3.1, 6.9 v4). For Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, per reporting on the Hitachi Energy advisory, the flaws are 2024 CVEs in the embedded GWS component, rated up to 9.9, affecting FCP 3.4.0 to 4.1.1 where GWS is installed; outlets disagree on fix availability, so work from Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229. Separately, CISA updated ICSA-26-211-07 on Mitsubishi Electric’s CC-Link IE TSN communication protocol the same day, adding eight affected products and removing three. CISA reports no known exploitation for anything in the batch. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 through ICSA-26-260-07 and the update to ICSA-26-211-07, taken from the cisagov CSAF files for 17 Sep 2026; Hitachi Energy FACTS detail per ISSSource and WindowsForum reporting on Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000229 - Released 17 Sep 2026; scores for -04 through -07 added 20 Sep 2026; bulletin count clarified as seven new plus one update 22 Sep 2026. No 22 Sep CISA batch was visible at generation time

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Secure FMC is under active exploitation by three clusters — one an APT whose tooling overlaps Sandworm’s, one a ransomware operator that deployed Qilin — on the box that manages your plant-boundary firewall policy
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, plant boundary
item.description: Cisco Talos reported on 9 September three clusters of post-compromise activity on on-premises Secure Firewall Management Center instances. UAT-12197 exploited CVE-2026-20079, the authentication-bypass flaw, and dropped a web shell, a JAR-based command executor and credential-exfiltration tooling; Talos names no actor behind it. UAT-11823, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be an advanced persistent threat actor, used both CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316 and deployed a variant of Cyclops Blink — tooling that overlaps Sandworm’s, which is not the same as attribution to Sandworm. UAT-11988, assessed with high confidence as a ransomware operator, got in only through CVE-2026-20316, a static-credential flaw, then ran reconnaissance, credential theft and tunnelling before ultimately deploying Qilin ransomware. BleepingComputer gives CVE-2026-20079 a CVSS score of 10.0 and CVE-2026-20316 a score of 5.3. On 16 September Cisco shipped the hardening release that accompanies the exploited FMC flaws, advisory cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN: eight internally found CVEs, CVE-2026-20329 through CVE-2026-20336, up to CVSS 9.9, with fixes across ASA, FTD and FMC; Cisco revised it on 18 September to update the ASA fixed-release table. The hardening CVEs themselves are not reported exploited. Talos does not mention OT, sectors or victim locations. The manufacturing relevance is position: FMC centrally manages the firewalls that commonly separate enterprise networks from plant zones, so an attacker holding it can read, and change, the rules that protect the plant. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; hardening release 16 Sep 2026, revised 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] One firmware, three vendors: IO-Link masters from Phoenix Contact, Pepperl+Fuchs and Carlo Gavazzi carry two CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated takeover flaws
item.category: Critical Advisory — Shared machine-level firmware, three vendors, no known exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published three coordinated advisories on 16 September for IO-Link master devices built on a common firmware below version 1.7.4: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8 (VDE-2026-027), Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2 and ICE3 modules (VDE-2026-014) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 devices (VDE-2026-028). The Pepperl+Fuchs advisory lists 22 CVEs and the Phoenix Contact advisory 20, with CVE-2026-27546 through CVE-2026-27565 running through the set, and the overlap is what points to a shared OEM firmware base rather than three separate defects. The flaws were found by Nozomi Networks Labs researchers. The two worst are rated CVSS 9.8: CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated operating-system command injection. Around them sit several CVSS 8.8 command-injection and local-file-inclusion flaws, an 8.1 authorisation bypass, a 7.5 path traversal and issues that expose password hashes and SSH private keys. Affected firmware is below 1.7.4 and the advisories name 1.7.8 as the fix. No exploitation has been reported. What makes this a manufacturing item is where the devices sit — at machine level, between the EtherNet/IP or PROFINET network and the sensors and actuators on the line — and the shared firmware, which puts one set of flaws on several brands of hardware at once. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-027 (Phoenix Contact), VDE-2026-014 (Pepperl+Fuchs) and VDE-2026-028 (Carlo Gavazzi); researcher credit per Nozomi Networks Labs - Published 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA’s 15 September batch: a CVSS 9.8 authorisation gap in mySCADA myPRO Manager, plus Siemens Mendix SAML and Teamcenter republished
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA released eight ICS advisories on 15 September, and three reach manufacturing environments. ICSA-26-258-03 covers mySCADA myPRO Manager 2.1 and earlier: CVE-2026-73807, a missing-authorisation flaw rated CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567, missing authentication for a critical function at 6.3, which could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a connected GSM modem. Version 2.2 fixes both, and CISA lists Critical Manufacturing among the affected sectors. ICSA-26-258-06 republishes Siemens SSA-887643: CVE-2026-80465 in Mendix SAML, CVSS 8.7, where improper signature verification allows account hijack in specific single-sign-on configurations, fixed in V3.6.27 and V4.2.3. ICSA-26-258-07 republishes Siemens SSA-157465, a reflected cross-site scripting flaw in Teamcenter’s /auth/ redirect, CVE-2026-58113 at 6.1, fixed in V2412.0013 and V2506.0010. CISA reports no known public exploitation of any of them. The same batch republished Schneider SCADAPack x70 and Siemens Reyrolle 7SR5 from the 8 September round, and CISA updated its Siemens OpenSSL and SICAM 8 advisories. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-258-03, ICSA-26-258-06 and ICSA-26-258-07, with Siemens ProductCERT SSA-887643 and SSA-157465 - Released 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Wibu CodeMeter flaws reach TRUMPF’s programming and production software — SYSTEM-level file deletion and possible remote command execution
item.category: Critical Advisory — Machine-tool programming software, third-party licensing component
item.description: TRUMPF disclosed through CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-091, dated 15 September, that TruTops Boost, TruTops Cell, TruTops Mark 3D, TruTops Weld, TecZone, Programming Tube, Oseon and TRUMPF License Expert are affected by five vulnerabilities in the Wibu CodeMeter Runtime licensing component on Windows, CVE-2026-81572 through CVE-2026-81576, rated up to CVSS 8.6. The flaws could allow file deletion with SYSTEM privileges, takeover of the CodeMeter WebAdmin interface and possibly remote command execution. The fix is to update CodeMeter Runtime to 9.10 on Windows 11 or 8.41a on Windows 10. No exploitation was noted. The exposure is on the Windows hosts that prepare and manage jobs for TRUMPF machines, which makes a compromised licensing service a foothold close to the machine tools. - TRUMPF security advisory via CERT@VDE VDE-2026-091 - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety — and a patch window measured in weeks to quarters, not days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Safety-rated PLC, no known exploitation
item.description: Schneider Electric’s advisory SEVD-2026-251-04 of 8 September discloses CVE-2026-3869, an incorrect implementation of an authentication algorithm (CWE-303) rated CVSS 9.2, in Modicon M580 controllers below application level 4.00 and Modicon M580 Safety below 4.20; Modicon MC80 is also affected. No exploitation has been reported. The reason this outranks the rest of the September batch on a manufacturing board is not the score but the asset class. M580 is one of the most widely deployed PLC families on discrete and process lines, and the Safety variant sits inside the protection layer, which means a firmware change is not a maintenance task but a revalidation exercise. Analysts covering the disclosure make the point plainly: for continuous-process plants the realistic interval between a vendor advisory and a validated, deployed fix on a safety-rated controller is measured in weeks to quarters, and the exposure runs for the whole of it. That gap, not the CVE, is the thing to manage. Treat the compensating controls as the actual remediation for this quarter and the firmware as the eventual close-out. - Schneider Electric security notification SEVD-2026-251-04 of 8 Sep 2026, with the patch-window analysis from the September 2026 ICS Patch Tuesday review - Advisory published 8 Sep 2026; analysis 9 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Siemens SIMOVE Fleetmanager and SIPLANT leak arbitrary files to an unauthenticated request — and SIPLANT has no fixed version yet
item.category: Critical Advisory — Fleet and plant asset management, one product still unfixed
item.description: CVE-2026-67367 is an unauthenticated relative path traversal in the embedded HTTP server that SIMOVE Fleetmanager (V3.1 through V4.0) and SIPLANT (V1.7 through V3.1) use to serve files. An attacker who can reach the service reads arbitrary files off the host without credentials; the flaw is scored 8.6 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.2 under v4.0. No exploitation has been reported. The detail that deserves attention is the split remediation status. Siemens has shipped fixes for SIMOVE Fleetmanager — 3.1.13, 3.2.4, 3.3.2 and 4.0.1 — but at the time of this edition there is no fixed version for SIPLANT, and the vendor directs affected users to support for mitigation. An arbitrary-file-read on an asset- and fleet-management server is rarely the objective in itself; it is a credential-harvesting step, because those servers hold configuration files, connection strings and service accounts that reach into the plant systems they inventory. CISA republished the Siemens advisory in its 22 September ICS batch, which puts it in front of teams that track CISA rather than Siemens ProductCERT; no exploitation has been reported since. - Siemens September 2026 advisory bundle for CVE-2026-67367, as catalogued by vulnerability-intelligence trackers citing the vendor advisory; CISA republication of 22 Sep 2026 per Chemical Facility Security News - Siemens published 8 Sep 2026; CISA republished 22 Sep 2026; SIPLANT shown as unfixed in the Siemens advisory of 8 Sep 2026, not re-checked for this edition

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and plant-floor teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. This is the plant-floor supply chain in its purest form. Self-hosted GitLab at manufacturers holds MES and ERP integration code, PLC project files checked in from engineering workstations, recipe and batch parameters, and the service-account credentials that let CI pipelines push to the shop floor. Reading files off that server is reconnaissance and credential theft in one step. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 work now totals twelve flaws — several chainable to root on the box aggregating your PROFINET traffic
item.category: Research — Siemens OT edge device, vendor-patched, no known exploitation
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, bringing the total to twelve vulnerabilities: nine in the device firmware, CVE-2025-40572 through CVE-2025-40580, scored between CVSS 5.3 and 8.5, and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, CVE-2025-40581 through CVE-2025-40583, scored 6.7 to 8.5. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 is affected, as is the Edge Client through V2.1; both are fixed in V4.0 HF0 and later, and Siemens has published an advisory and patches. The finding that matters operationally is that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which Nozomi describes as enabling manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onward. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth getting right, because they have been reported loosely elsewhere. The first part of this research, four PROFINET DCP memory-corruption flaws each rated CVSS 5.3, was published on 10 September and covers CVEs originally disclosed in May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was CISA updating that advisory to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes, not a new critical flaw. Note also that the CVE identifiers carry 2025 prefixes although the disclosure is 2026, which is consistent with how this research line was assigned; check them against the Siemens advisory before you feed them into a scanner. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, part two — reporting via Industrial Cyber; related CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 and the Siemens ProductCERT advisory for the same devices - Part one 10 Sep 2026; CISA advisory update 15 Sep 2026; part two published 18 Sep 2026; underlying CVEs first disclosed May 2025

item.title: [High] A CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated root flaw in Check Point’s Security Management Server — the box that writes your plant-boundary firewall policy
item.category: Critical Advisory — Firewall management plane, unexploited
item.description: Check Point has fixed CVE-2026-91843, a stack overflow in the login process of its Security Management and Log Servers that an unauthenticated request carrying an overly long username can use to run code as root. It is rated CVSS 9.8, and Check Point states there is no indication it has been exploited in the wild. Reporting on the advisory (sk1000155) lists affected builds as R82.10 up to Jumbo Hotfix Take 44, R82 up to Take 126, all R82.20 builds, R81.20 up to Take 166, R81.10 up to Take 190, and the end-of-support R81 and R80.x lines; Multi-Domain Server is affected, and Smart-1 Cloud is already fixed. The Hacker News reports that a Trusted Clients misconfiguration is a precondition; that detail could not be checked against the vendor text, so treat it as a reason to review the setting rather than as a reason to wait. This is a separate flaw from the gateway VPN vulnerabilities on the card below, and also separate from CVE-2026-93616, a different Management Server flaw that Check Point confirmed on 22 September had been exploited as a zero-day since July (see the card above); 91843 itself is still not reported as exploited. For a manufacturer the weight comes from position: the management server holds and pushes the policy for every gateway it manages, including the ones separating enterprise networks from plant zones, so control of it is control of the plant boundary. - Check Point advisory sk1000155 as reported by The Hacker News (17 Sep 2026) and SecurityWeek (18 Sep 2026); the vendor page itself could not be retrieved for this edition - Reported 17 Sep 2026; SecurityWeek round-up 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Check Point confirms exploitation of its CVSS 9.8 gateway VPN flaw since 12 September — now in KEV with a 25 September deadline
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: The warning the Dutch NCSC issued on 12 September has been overtaken. Check Point’s own advisory of 22 September states that, starting 12 September 2026, it observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers using CVE-2026-85102 — improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls, rated CVSS 9.8, which allows unauthenticated remote code execution. Check Point released the fix on 9 September, so the flaw was patched before exploitation began; it gives no customer count and no attribution. It has published indicators: exploitation certificates with subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, OU=users, O=global. CISA added CVE-2026-85102 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 22 September with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. The companion flaw the NCSC also named, CVE-2026-85103, has not been reported as exploited. For a manufacturer the exposure is the plant-to-plant and plant-to-vendor topology behind the gateway: site-to-site tunnels linking factories to the corporate datacentre and to MES, ERP and PLM, plus the OEM and integrator paths to engineering workstations, robot controllers and line HMIs. Spark appliances are the small-site and branch boxes most likely to front a single plant or warehouse. A gateway compromise does not stop a line by itself, but it puts an attacker on the wrong side of the only boundary most plants have. - Check Point security advisory of 22 Sep 2026 (vendor blog) and the CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026; the earlier Dutch NCSC warning as reported by BleepingComputer (12 Sep 2026) - Fixes released 9 Sep 2026; exploitation from 12 Sep 2026; KEV listing 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Five more exploited flaws enter KEV — and two of them sit in the toolchain that builds and supports your plant
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, build and remote-support tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September after evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to obtain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. Both land squarely in manufacturing’s soft spots. Artifactory is where many engineering organisations store the container images, libraries and firmware packages that end up on MES servers, edge gateways and line controllers — a poisoned artefact there reaches the plant on the next deployment. ScreenConnect and its equivalents are how machine builders and integrators reach engineering workstations, often installed at commissioning and never inventoried. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13, 14 and 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September ICS Patch Tuesday hits the plant patch window — Siemens, Schneider and Aveva criticals, and one flaw already exploited
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch batch, one chained item exploited
item.description: Siemens published seven advisories on 8 September, including critical fixes in Industrial Edge Management and Open Interface Services and a fourteen-CVE set for Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays led by an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8. Schneider Electric issued four the same day, headed by a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2, with PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert also patched. Aveva fixed four flaws in Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key. None of that is exploited. What is exploited is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a CVSS 10 pre-authentication remote code execution flaw added to KEV the same day — the remote-monitoring platform many MSP-managed plants inherit. Stacked on last week’s Rockwell batch, that is a lot of controller and engineering-workstation work chasing very few outage windows. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 and Schneider Electric security notifications of 8 Sep 2026, summarised by SecurityWeek; N-central exploitation status from the CISA KEV catalog and N-able - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; CISA formalised the Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor fixes as ICSA-26-253-01 on 10 Sep 2026, reporting no known exploitation

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth RCE in the remote-monitoring platform your MSP runs, plus two Windows zero-days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Four actively exploited flaws added to CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog on 8 September. The one that reaches plants is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 giving unauthenticated remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against the platform’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and the vendor shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — a fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal deadline was 11 September and has now passed. Two Windows privilege-escalation zero-days were added the same day, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, along with CVE-2026-75650 in Adobe Commerce. N-central matters here because a managed-service console is a standing path onto engineering workstations at plants that outsource IT. - CISA KEV catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with vendor confirmation from N-able, Microsoft and Adobe and telemetry reported by Huntress - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; federal deadline 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A malformed CIP message faults ControlLogix and CompactLogix controllers until someone power-cycles them
item.category: Critical Advisory — Controller fault requiring a power cycle
item.description: ICSA-26-244-03 covers CVE-2026-9637, an improper input-length validation flaw in CIP message processing rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 and CVSS v4.0 8.7. A crafted message drives ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380 controllers into a major non-recoverable fault, and recovery requires a physical power cycle — which on most lines means an unplanned stop and, for the GuardLogix families, a safety-function interruption. Rockwell has published fixed firmware. One point needs care: Rockwell’s own advisory header describes the issue as exploited, but SecurityWeek reports this is likely a documentation error, and CISA states it is unaware of exploitation. We report it as not known to be exploited, and would treat any contrary vendor confirmation as the trigger to escalate. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-244-03 and the Rockwell Automation security advisory — exploitation status per CISA, with SecurityWeek reporting the vendor header as a likely documentation error - Advisory published 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Guidance] NIST opens SP 800-82 Rev. 4 for comment — the baseline OT security guide, rebuilt around CSF 2.0 and zero trust
item.category: Guidance — NIST OT security guide, draft for public comment
item.description: NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Revision 4, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, on 21 September, with comments due by 30 November 2026. The revision restructures the guide around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, moving risk management under the CSF Govern function; adds security-architecture guidance focused on protecting system-management functions and applying zero-trust principles; expands guidance on implementing OT controls, including asset management and network monitoring and detection; and widens scope to building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and IIoT and cloud convergence. It is a draft, so nothing in it binds anyone yet. For manufacturers the practical point is that 800-82 is the document auditors, insurers and customers reach for when they ask how an OT programme is structured, and a revision reorganised around CSF 2.0 will change the vocabulary of those questions. - NIST CSRC publication page for SP 800-82r4 ipd (primary, read 24 Sep 2026) — reported by Industrial Cyber (22 Sep 2026) - Draft released 21 Sep 2026; comments due 30 Nov 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA makes the case for decoys and tripwires — the rare detection measure you can add without touching a running process
item.category: Guidance — CISA, detection and response
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September, guidance built on the assumption that an adversary will eventually obtain some access to your network and that you should be prepared to notice. It defines decoys as assets that appear legitimate — systems, accounts or data — but exist to distract an adversary, reveal their presence, or collect intelligence about them, and recommends tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens alongside a Zero Trust posture. The guide plans the work around the three MITRE Engage goals of Expose, Affect and Elicit, maps the resulting detections to ATT&CK, and pays particular attention to the gaps left by living-off-the-land activity, which conventional signature detection handles poorly. It sets out three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — and asks for continuous iteration with red teaming. Industrial Cyber reports that the guidance includes a detailed water and wastewater case study covering decoys for OT HMIs; SecurityWeek’s coverage does not mention water or OT, so treat the OT case study as that outlet’s reporting. The reason this belongs on a manufacturing page is its cost profile. Nearly every detection improvement offered to a plant requires touching something that is running. A decoy engineering workstation, a fake historian credential or an unused PLC-style address that nothing legitimate should ever touch adds detection without altering the process, and anything that queries it is worth a phone call by definition. - CISA guidance “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reporting via Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek; the CISA PDF was not retrieved directly - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA is retiring its weekly Vulnerability Summary on 28 September — check whether your patch process quietly depends on it
item.category: Policy — CISA, vulnerability data sources
item.description: CISA will discontinue its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September, pointing users instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and its advisories, which continue unchanged. The move is framed as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation direction set in BOD 26-04 in June 2026: rather than a comprehensive weekly list of everything published, attention goes to what is demonstrably being exploited. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. For a manufacturer this is an administrative item with one practical edge. Vulnerability-management routines accumulate quiet dependencies, and in plenty of organisations somebody’s Monday morning begins by opening that bulletin, or a script parses it into a ticket queue. If that is true for you, the feed stops in under two weeks and the replacement is not like-for-like: KEV is deliberately narrower, so a process rebuilt on KEV alone will see less. Reported here as a factual change to a data source, without comment on the underlying policy direction. - CISA announcement of the weekly Vulnerability Summary retirement — reported by SecurityWeek; the CISA page was not retrieved directly - Reported 17 Sep 2026; effective 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Manufacturers sit on both sides of this. Any product with digital elements that you place on the EU market makes you the regulated party; everything you buy for the plant floor makes you the beneficiary of somebody else's new reporting duty. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Medium] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting is live — and if your product has a chip in it, this one is aimed at you
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force, applies to manufacturers directly
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with detail on the exploit and mitigation status, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available, as well as informing affected users. The obligations reach any manufacturer placing products on the EU market regardless of where it is based, with penalties up to €15 million. Unlike most items on this page, this is not something happening to your suppliers — if you build machinery, instruments, vehicles, appliances, medical devices or any connected product sold into Europe, the 24-hour clock is now yours. It also improves what you receive: your own automation vendors are on the same clock. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Guidance] NIST finalises IR 8536 — a way to answer “where did this component actually come from?” without one central database
item.category: Guidance — NIST supply-chain traceability framework for manufacturers
item.description: NIST has published the finalised version of IR 8536, a technology-neutral meta-framework for organising, linking and querying supply-chain traceability data across different systems and stakeholders without requiring a centralised repository. Its purpose is to let manufacturers assemble verifiable end-to-end provenance chains — raw material through fabrication, assembly, ship and receive — using interoperable event templates that different parties can each hold in their own systems. For supply-chain risk management that translates into two concrete questions becoming answerable: whether a component is counterfeit or substituted, and whether a piece of hardware or firmware entered the build without authorisation. This is standards guidance, not an advisory and not a response to an active threat; there is no CVE, no deadline and nothing to patch. It is worth a slot on a manufacturing board because component provenance is the control that sits underneath several of the threats already on this page — the PLM and engineering-data campaigns, and the integrator and machine-builder access paths that keep showing up as the way in. - NIST IR 8536 final publication — reported by Industrial Cyber - Finalised and reported 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Policy] 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules across 27 agencies — and the hours they take out of your response
item.category: Regulation — Federal cyber incident reporting
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, using GAO figures, count 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of them applying to private industry. Their argument is operational: in the first hours of an incident the same handful of people is asked to satisfy several overlapping obligations on different clocks and in different formats, and that effort comes straight out of response. The timing matters because CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. Manufacturers are not lightly regulated here either — a multi-site producer can face CIRCIA, sector-specific rules for chemicals or defence work, state breach statutes, customer contractual notice clauses, and from 11 September the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s 24-hour reporting duty for its own products. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO counts, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published and reported 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026
